



Independent Submission                                             S. Li
Internet-Draft                                   RTTP & IQA Organization
Intended status: Informational                           1 November 2026
Expires: 5 May 2027


  The rttp and iqa URI Schemes: Derived-Address Intent and Attestation
                               Addressing
                    draft-li-rttp-iqa-addressing-02

Abstract

   This document specifies two companion URI schemes built on one shared
   addressing model, in which the address of a subject is derived by
   computation from the authority and no lookup service, registry, or
   name-resolution system is consulted when the URI is used.  The "rttp"
   scheme names a claim of intent directed at an identified subject; the
   "iqa" scheme names the attestation standing of an identified subject,
   as reported by one of three named organs, and carries no proof and no
   credential.  The two are deliberately paired: intent addressing
   carries the claim, attestation carries whether the claimant is
   verified.

   Both schemes parse fail-closed, and the document states the
   requirements a client MUST satisfy when it handles such URIs, to
   avoid the failure modes that short, user-embeddable strings invite:
   using the authority as a navigation target (open redirect), using a
   registered handler as a general-purpose launcher, and, for "iqa", a
   parse that looks like a certification.

   The document specifies three components that companion
   implementations already run: a trust lease, which carries the
   freshness of every attestation answer in-band and is checked against
   the verifier's own clock, offline; two fixed-length wire formats, the
   128-octet pulse header of the "rttp" scheme and the 128-octet
   attestation envelope of the "iqa" scheme; and a closed refusal
   vocabulary with grant references for attestation responses.  This
   revision adds to these the rules for when the facts a verification
   consumes are evaluated — at the moment of use, not the moment of
   grant — and how any policy interpreter relates to the answer it
   consumes.

   This document is not an Internet Standard.  It is an Informational
   specification of two experimental addressing schemes, published for
   the public record.

1.  Introduction

   Most URI schemes name a location: the authority identifies a host to
   be contacted.  This document specifies two schemes that name
   something else.  The "rttp" scheme names a claim of intent directed
   at an identified subject.  The "iqa" scheme names the attestation
   standing of an identified subject, as reported by a named organ.  In
   both cases, what a client does with what the URI names is defined by
   the scheme; where the subject might be reached is not part of the URI
   and is not resolved through any lookup service.

   The two schemes share one addressing model and are deliberately
   paired: intent addressing carries the claim, attestation carries
   whether the claimant is verified.  Implementations and deployments
   should treat them as one model rather than as two unrelated
   namespaces.

   Four properties follow from the shared model and are normative in
   this document:

   *  the address is *derived by computation* from the authority
      (Sections 4.4 and 5.1);

   *  there is *no lookup*: no DNS, no registry query, no fetch
      (Sections 4.5 and 5.5);

   *  the URI is a *claim, not a proof* (Sections 5.2 and 9);

   *  both schemes fail closed: non-conforming input is rejected, never
      repaired (Sections 4 and 5).

   *Naming note.* IQA denotes *Identity* Quality Assurance.  It is not
   affiliated with the *Institute* of Quality Assurance (which became
   the Chartered Quality Institute in 2007), nor is it the computer-
   vision field of *Image* Quality Assessment.  RTTP denotes *Resonant
   Time Transfer Protocol*.  It is not RTP: what it names is a claim,
   not a session or a data stream.














Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                   [Page 4]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


   Addressing alone leaves two questions unanswered: how fresh is the
   answer a verifier relies on, and in what bytes do the schemes travel?
   This document answers both.  Section 6 defines the trust lease, the
   freshness semantics that the schemes' name promises and that deployed
   implementations already perform; Section 7 defines the two fixed-
   length wire formats; Section 8 defines the response vocabulary of an
   attestation.  All three components are codifications of behaviour
   that implementations already exhibit; this document defines no new
   mechanism for its own sake.  This revision adds no mechanism either:
   it fixes when the facts those components consume are evaluated — at
   the moment of use, not the moment of grant (Section 6.3) — and how a
   policy interpreter relates to the answer it consumes (Section 8.4).

2.  Conventions and Terminology

   The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT",
   "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and
   "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP
   14 [RFC2119] [RFC8174] when, and only when, they appear in all
   capitals, as shown here.

   This document uses the ABNF notation of [RFC5234] and the URI syntax
   of [RFC3986].

   Terminology:

   *authority* — The three-segment component of either scheme:
   <intent>.<pillar>.<root> for "rttp" (Section 4.1) and
   <subject>.<organ>.<root> for "iqa" (Section 5.1).  It is a name, not
   a host name, and is never resolved.

   *subject* — The entity a URI names or is directed at.  It is a claim
   about which identity is of interest, not a proof of that identity.

   *organ* — The segment that identifies the subject or answers for it:
   in "rttp", a readable token (readable form of intent) or a fixed-
   width derived value (hash form); in "iqa", one of three defined names
   (Section 5.1).

   *root* — The root label of the "iqa" authority.  It is a name and is
   not resolved.

   *claim of intent* — A statement that a subject intends an action.  It
   is a claim, not evidence, and establishes no identity by itself.







Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                   [Page 5]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


   *standing* — The attestation answer an organ returns for a subject.
   The values it may take form the closed set fixed in Section 7.2;
   their semantics are the business of the reference specification
   [IQA-SPEC].  It carries the attestation algorithm, the standing
   vocabulary and the conformance material.

   *standing read* — A read of a subject's current attestation answer
   from the named organ, as in the default operation of Section 5.3.  It
   is a safe, read-only operation.

   *trust lease* — The freshness window carried in-band by an
   attestation answer, and the mechanism of Section 6 by which a
   verifier decides whether an answer may be relied on.

   *pulse header* — The fixed-length wire format that carries the "rttp"
   scheme (Section 7.1).

   *attestation envelope* — The fixed-length wire format that carries an
   "iqa" attestation answer (Section 7.2).

   *refusal reason* — The closed vocabulary by which an attestation
   response states that, and only that, an answer was refused
   (Section 8.1).

   *grant reference* — The structure by which an attestation response
   names the authorisation it relied on (Section 8.2).

   *action* — The optional final path segment naming what is claimed to
   be intended ("rttp") or an operation requested of the organ ("iqa").

   *fail closed* — To reject non-conforming input rather than repair,
   normalise, or fall back: both schemes fail closed at parse time
   (Sections 4 and 5), and both wire formats fail closed on length,
   magic, and version (Section 7).

   *derived address* — The 16-octet value computed from the authority
   alone (Section 4.4): the first 16 octets of the SHA-256 digest of the
   canonical authority.  It is deterministic, pure computation, one-way,
   and action-independent, and it is an entry fingerprint, not a proof
   of identity.  The same value appears at a fixed offset in both wire
   formats (Section 7).

   *ROUTE_SHARD* — The 16-byte value derived from the "rttp" authority
   as specified in Section 4.4.







Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                   [Page 6]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


   *AID* — A self-certifying subject identifier defined outside this
   document.  Nothing here depends on an AID registry or authority, and
   no assumption is made about its length or encoding beyond what
   Sections 4.2, 5.2 and 9 require.

3.  The Shared Addressing Model

   Both schemes defined in this document instantiate one addressing
   model, whose four properties are stated in Section 1 and made
   normative per scheme in Sections 4 and 5: the address is derived by
   computation rather than assigned; every segment of an authority is a
   name, never a host; a URI is a claim, never a proof; and both schemes
   fail closed.

   The model is deliberately minimal: no discovery mechanism, no
   transport, no key directory, no authorisation decision, and no
   registry of any kind is defined.  What is defined is the grammar, the
   derivation, and the minimum client behaviour that make the two
   schemes safe to embed.

4.  The rttp URI Scheme

   The rttp scheme is the where and the when of a claim.  Its authority
   is the derived address of a subject (Section 4.4), and its action
   names what is claimed to be intended (Section 4.1).  The when of the
   claim is not part of the URI: it is stated by the pulse that carries
   the derived address on the wire (Section 7.1.2).  Where the pulse and
   an attestation answer agree, action begins (Section 7).

4.1.  Syntax

   The general form of an rttp URI is:

   rttp://<intent>.<pillar>.<root>[/<action>]

   The authority is exactly three dot-separated segments:

   *  intent: 8 lowercase hexadecimal digits (a derived value), or a
      readable operator-chosen label; both forms are opaque to a client.

   *  pillar: an operator-chosen label.  No enumeration of pillar labels
      and no registry for them is defined.

   *  root: an operator-chosen label matching 1*( %x61-7A / DIGIT / "-"
      ).

   The action, when present, is a single path segment: "/" 1*( %x61-7A /
   DIGIT / "-" ).



Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                   [Page 7]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


   ABNF:

   rttp-URI     = "rttp://" authority [ "/" action ]
   authority    = intent "." pillar "." root
   intent       = hash-intent / name-intent
   hash-intent  = 8 lowhex
   name-intent  = 1*( %x61-7A / DIGIT / "-" )
   pillar       = 1*( %x61-7A / DIGIT / "-" )
   root         = 1*( %x61-7A / DIGIT / "-" )
   action       = 1*( %x61-7A / DIGIT / "-" )
   lowhex       = %x30-39 / %x61-66

   The examples below use reserved names per [RFC2606]; operators use
   labels they control:

   rttp://f3b2a1c4.pillar.example/vessel
   rttp://organ.pillar.example/verify
   rttp://f3b2a1c4.pillar.example

4.2.  Reserved Characters and Exclusions

   These exclusions apply to both schemes.  Section 5.2 adds the ones
   specific to "iqa".

   *  The canonical form is *lowercase US-ASCII*.  Uppercase is *invalid
      input*, not a formatting difference: a parser MUST NOT normalise
      it, because two distinct strings would then map onto one address.

   *  ., / and :// are the delimiters defined by these schemes.

   *  Neither scheme defines *userinfo, port, query or fragment*.  A URI
      carrying any of them is not valid, and a fragment MUST NOT be used
      to address an action.  Credentials cannot appear in such a URI,
      and there is no field in which to exfiltrate data.

   *  Percent-encoding follows Section 2.1 of [RFC3986].  No component
      requires characters outside the unreserved set, so a canonical URI
      contains no percent-encoded octets; a parser MAY reject such input
      rather than normalising it.

   *  There is *no "rttps"* scheme and no fallback.  A client that does
      not implement this scheme fails closed (Section 4.5).

4.3.  Default Operation

   Dereferencing an rttp URI without an action requests the *default
   operation*: one single round-trip semantic request against the
   subject named by the authority.



Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                   [Page 8]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


   The default operation is *safe* in the sense of Section 9.2.1 of
   [RFC9110]: it creates no obligations and mutates no state of the
   subject.

   When an action is present, the default operation is not implied for
   it.  An action names _what_ is claimed to be intended; the safety of
   a given action is not defined by this document, and a client MUST NOT
   infer safety from this section; see Section 9.

4.4.  The Address: ROUTE_SHARD Derivation

   The routing address of an rttp URI is derived from the authority
   alone:

   canonical_authority = intent "." pillar "." root
                         (lowercase, US-ASCII)
   ROUTE_SHARD         = SHA-256(ASCII(canonical_authority))[0:16]

   The *authority only*: the scheme name, "//" and any action are
   excluded.

   The derived address has four properties: it is *deterministic* (the
   same authority always yields the same address); it is *pure
   computation* (no DNS, no registry, no network access, no lookup
   service); it is *one-way* (the authority cannot be recovered from the
   address); and it is *action-independent* (different actions on one
   authority yield the same address).

   The last property is why an action is not part of the addressing
   component: *an address is _where_, not _what_ — and not _when_*; the
   pulse that carries the address states when the claim was made
   (Section 7.1.2).  Were the action to participate in derivation, two
   actions on one subject would become two addresses, splitting one
   subject into several.

   A client MUST NOT perform a lookup in order to use an rttp URI
   (Section 4.5).

4.5.  Client Requirements

   A client that handles an rttp or iqa URI (including a resolver page,
   a protocol handler, and a library that renders one) MUST satisfy the
   requirements below.  They follow from Section 9: either URI may be
   supplied by an untrusted party, and what it names is a claim rather
   than a proof.  Section 5.5 adds the one requirement specific to
   "iqa".





Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                   [Page 9]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


4.5.1.  No Navigation to the URI

   A client MUST NOT use any component of an rttp or iqa URI as a
   navigation target.  A client that renders a link, redirect, or fetch
   derived from any such URI is an *open redirect* and is non-
   conformant; a client MAY navigate only to a destination that is fixed
   in advance by the client itself.

4.5.2.  Scheme Prefix Check

   A protocol handler MUST reject any input whose scheme is neither rttp
   nor iqa nor the exact scheme name under which that handler was itself
   registered; without this check it becomes a general-purpose launcher
   that any page can use to open an arbitrary URI of any scheme.

4.5.3.  Consent, Never Silence

   The ability to handle rttp or iqa URIs MUST NOT be acquired without
   an explicit action by the user, and a client MUST NOT simulate, pre-
   select, or otherwise bypass that consent.  Where the platform exposes
   the list of registered handlers, that list MUST NOT be exposed to the
   network.

4.5.4.  No Lookup

   A client MUST NOT perform a lookup in order to use an rttp or iqa
   URI: no DNS query, no registry query, and no fetch of any resource
   named or implied by the URI.  Use of either scheme is a local
   computation (Section 3); there is no resolver to poison and no
   registration to hijack (Section 9).

5.  The iqa URI Scheme

   The iqa scheme is the whether of a claim: it names a subject and the
   organ to ask about that subject's standing.  The URI itself carries
   no verdict and no credential (Section 5.5.1); the verdict arrives as
   an attestation answer whose freshness is the lease of Section 6.

5.1.  Syntax

   The general form of an iqa URI is:

   iqa://<subject>.<organ>.<root>[/<action>]

   The authority comprises exactly three dot-separated segments, in this
   order:





Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                  [Page 10]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


   *  subject: 8, 32 or 64 lowercase hexadecimal digits (a derived
      routing hash), or a readable label; both forms are opaque to a
      client.

   *  organ: one of the three organ names, forge, tss or gateway.  This
      is a *closed set*; no other value is valid.

   *  root: the root label of this scheme.  Like every other segment it
      is a name and is never resolved.

   The action, when present, is a single path segment and is one of the
   four operation names verify, audit, attest or revoke.  This is also a
   *closed set*.

   ABNF:

   iqa-URI       = "iqa://" iqa-authority [ "/" iqa-action ]
   iqa-authority = subject "." organ "." iqa-root
   subject       = hash-subject / name-subject
   hash-subject  = 8( iqa-lowhex ) / 32( iqa-lowhex ) / 64( iqa-lowhex )
   name-subject  = 1*( %x61-7A / DIGIT / "-" )
   organ         = "forge" / "tss" / "gateway"
   iqa-root      = 1*( %x61-7A / DIGIT / "-" )
   iqa-action    = "verify" / "audit" / "attest" / "revoke"
   iqa-lowhex    = DIGIT / %x61-66

   Examples (the examples use the root label of this specification and
   placeholder subjects):

   iqa://3f9a1b2c.gateway.iqa (routing hash, standing read)
   iqa://0000004149434e531c5b21d80403358b.forge.iqa
   iqa://3f9a1b2c.tss.iqa/audit (explicit fidelity audit)
   iqa://master-authority.gateway.iqa/verify (readable label form)

5.2.  Reserved Characters and Exclusions

   The exclusions of Section 4.2 apply to iqa URIs as they do to rttp
   URIs.  Two are specific to this scheme:

   *  There is *no "iqas"* scheme and no protocol fallback.  A client
      that does not implement this scheme fails closed (Section 5.5).

   *  The hexadecimal subject form is a *routing hint, not evidence*. It
      carries no verification weight; identity is bound outside the URI
      and is never established by parsing one (Section 9).






Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                  [Page 11]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


5.3.  Default Operation

   Dereferencing an iqa URI without an action requests the *default
   operation*: a standing read, returning the subject's current
   attestation answer as reported by the named organ.

   The default operation is *safe* in the sense of Section 9.2.1 of
   [RFC9110]: it creates no obligation, transfers no value, and mutates
   no state.

   The following rule is normative:

   *Dereferencing an iqa URI, by itself, MUST NOT transition any
   subject's standing state.*

   When an action is present, the default operation is not implied for
   it.  Which actions are safe is stated in Section 5.4; a client MUST
   NOT infer safety for an unrecognised verb (Section 9).

5.4.  Action Safety Classes

   The four defined actions, and the omitted-action form, have the
   following classes:

   audit is not classified safe because the measurement it requests can
   itself change the outcome it measures.  audit, attest and revoke MUST
   be requested explicitly and MUST NOT be reachable by dereferencing a
   URI that omits the action.























Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                  [Page 12]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


      +===========+==========================+=====================+
      | Action    | Semantics                | Class               |
      +===========+==========================+=====================+
      | (omitted) | Read the current         | *SAFE*, read-only   |
      |           | standing.                |                     |
      +-----------+--------------------------+---------------------+
      | verify    | Compare a presented seal | *SAFE*, read-only   |
      |           | against the subject.  No | comparison          |
      |           | state is written.        |                     |
      +-----------+--------------------------+---------------------+
      | audit     | Request a fidelity       | *NOT SAFE*, a       |
      |           | measurement of the       | failed measurement  |
      |           | subject's execution.     | may change standing |
      +-----------+--------------------------+---------------------+
      | attest    | Request that a seal be   | *NOT SAFE*, state   |
      |           | issued for the subject.  | transition          |
      +-----------+--------------------------+---------------------+
      | revoke    | Withdraw the subject's   | *NOT SAFE*, state   |
      |           | standing.                | transition          |
      +-----------+--------------------------+---------------------+

                                 Table 1

5.5.  Client Requirements

   The client requirements of Section 4.5 apply to iqa URIs as they do
   to rttp URIs: no navigation to the URI, a scheme prefix check, no
   lookup, and consent that is never silent.  One requirement is
   specific to this scheme: parsing is not attestation.

5.5.1.  Parsing Is Not Attestation

   A client that displays a parsed or rendered iqa URI MUST NOT present
   the result as evidence of standing.  Reading the syntax establishes
   nothing about any subject; standing is established only by the answer
   of the named organ, under the rules of the reference specification
   [IQA-SPEC].

6.  Trust Lease and Freshness

   An attestation answer is only useful for as long as it is fresh.
   This section defines how freshness is carried and checked.  The
   mechanism described here is the one companion implementations already
   perform; what this section adds is the name and the rules.







Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                  [Page 13]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


6.1.  The Lease

   Every attestation answer produced under the iqa scheme carries its
   freshness window in-band: the answer states the instant until which
   it may be relied on, in a field of the answer itself (the
   lease_expiry field of Section 7.2), not in a cache header, a lookup
   result, or an out-of-band agreement.

   A verifier checks the stated expiry against its own clock.  The check
   is local and offline: no network call is involved in deciding whether
   an answer is fresh.  An answer whose lease has expired MUST be
   treated as expired; a verifier MUST NOT extend, renew, or reinterpret
   an expired lease except by obtaining a new answer.

   The window is short by design.  Current deployments use 120 seconds.
   The number constrains the verifier's honesty, not the speed of any
   channel: a verifier that accepts a statement older than its lease is
   asserting more than it knows.  Operators MAY configure other window
   lengths; the mechanism does not depend on this value.  Whether the
   lease instant itself counts as fresh or as expired is a deployment
   convention; implementations SHOULD declare which boundary they use,
   and conformance material MAY test both.

6.2.  Answer Modes

   A deployment declares one of two modes for standing reads, and each
   run or deployment SHOULD state which mode it operates in.  The two
   modes are distinguishable by more than a flag: under the same
   revocation timeline they yield different answers, because the live
   read reports the revocation itself while the cached answer can only
   report that current validity is not established.

   *cached-lease mode* — The verifier relies on a previously obtained
   answer whose lease (Section 6.1) has not expired, checked locally and
   offline: establishing that the evidence is fresh requires no network
   call, and this property is the design point of the mode, not a
   degradation.  A cached answer is, however, as-of an earlier instant:
   it does not by itself establish the subject's current validity, and
   the mode makes no claim that it does.  Whether an action proceeds on
   lease-fresh evidence is decided by the calling layer's action policy,
   not by this document: a policy that demands a current observation
   refuses the call with authority_not_determined (Section 8.1); a
   policy that accepts lease-fresh evidence may admit it, with any
   exposure bounded by the lease itself.







Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                  [Page 14]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


   *live-standing-read mode* — The verifier consults the named organ at
   the time of each request.  If the organ cannot be reached, the read
   fails closed: an organ that cannot be reached is not read as silent
   consent.  Every call in this mode is expected to be refused when the
   organ is unreachable, regardless of the age of any cached answer.

   In both modes the following rules are normative: an answer whose
   lease has expired MUST be refused; and an organ that cannot be
   reached MUST NOT be read as affirmative standing (Section 9.2).

   The modes also settle the mid-task case.  A condition that only has
   to hold when the delegation is made can be checked once; a condition
   that has to hold at every later use is re-checked at each use, and
   the lease is what makes the re-check possible without a network call.
   When a lease expires mid-task — an employee whose authority has
   ended, a grant whose window has closed — the next verification
   answers authority_revoked or evidence_expired (Section 8.1); the
   caller that holds the answer has held its expiry timestamp since that
   first answer, and can arm its halt at the boundary before the
   boundary arrives.  The physical act of halting remains enforcement
   and stays with the calling layer.  The condition may belong to the
   delegator's policy; the freshness of the facts that policy consumes
   comes from the wire.

6.3.  Evaluation at the Moment of Use

   An access policy is expressed when the delegation is made; the
   condition it states is judged when the resource is invoked.  This
   document fixes only the second moment: the facts a condition consumes
   — who the subject is, and whether that subject's authority stands
   verified — MUST be re-derivable at the moment of use, and the lease
   and its expiry timestamp (Section 6.1) are what carry that re-
   derivability.  A condition evaluated only at grant time says nothing
   about the state of the world at invocation.

   The boundary case is stated honestly rather than wished away.  A
   revocation that arrives just before, or just after, an invocation
   ends is a boundary no protocol can erase; the wire's job is to make
   that boundary legible.  An answer read past its expiry MUST be
   answered as expired (Section 8.1), never replayed as fresh.  Where an
   answer cannot arrive in time, the deployment's declared mode
   (Section 6.2) and the residual treatment of Section 6.4 apply: the
   bytes state how old the claim is, so the caller decides with the age
   on the table instead of on a silent assumption.







Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                  [Page 15]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


6.4.  Out of Scope

   Store-and-forward and archival uses — cases in which a statement is
   verified long after its lease has expired, with its age stated in the
   bytes rather than checked against a window — are the lease's residual
   treatment; they are not defined by this document.  They do not
   contradict the lease: a statement that makes no freshness claim is
   never falsified by one.

7.  Wire Formats

   The two schemes are carried by two fixed-length wire formats, one per
   scheme.  Both are 128 octets long, both encode multi-octet integers
   as unsigned big-endian (network byte order), and both fail closed: a
   receiver MUST reject any frame whose length is not exactly 128
   octets, or whose magic or version it does not know.

   They share one design decision: the derived address of a subject
   appears at a fixed offset in both formats, and it is the same
   16-octet value derived in Section 4.4.  One subject has one derived
   address and two carriers.  This overlap is by design and is not a
   compatibility claim.

   The two formats also split the WHEN of a claim between them, and the
   split is the pairing in miniature.  The pulse states when it was
   emitted: TIMESTAMP is an absolute time in nanoseconds
   (Section 7.1.2).  The answer states until when it may be relied on:
   lease_expiry (Section 7.2), checked under the rules of Section 6.1.
   Neither field authorizes anything by itself.  An action begins where
   the two agree: the subject named by the pulse and the subject bound
   by the answer are the same 16-octet derived address, and the moment
   the pulse claims falls within the answer's lease.  What proceeds from
   that agreement is the calling layer's decision (Sections 6.2 and 8);
   the schemes' job is to make the where, the when, and the whether
   trustworthy and cheap.

7.1.  The Pulse Header (rttp)

   The pulse header is the fixed 128-octet structure that carries an
   rttp pulse.  Its fields are fixed-offset, so a reader validates a
   header with fixed comparisons rather than by parsing a variable
   layout.









Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                  [Page 16]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


   Offset  Len  Field         Description
   0x00     4   RTTP_MAGIC    0x52545450 (ASCII "RTTP")
   0x04    16   VERSION_ID    Format version; 130 in this revision
   0x14    16   SEQUENCE_ID   Monotonic per-sender pulse index
   0x24    16   TIMESTAMP     Absolute emission time in nanoseconds
   0x34     1   TTL_PULSE     Hop count; a receiver decrements and
                              drops the pulse at zero
   0x35     1   PRIORITY      Operator-assigned scheduling weight
   0x36    16   ROUTE_SHARD   The derived address of the subject
                              (Section 4.4)
   0x46    32   AID_ORIGIN    The subject's AID (Section 2)
   0x66    26   (extension)   The extension block of Section 7.1.1;
                              all zero when absent

7.1.1.  The Extension Block

   The 26 octets at offsets 0x66-0x7F were reserved and all-zero in
   versions before the extension.  The extension block occupies them
   without moving or redefining any earlier field, and VERSION_ID is not
   incremented: implementations that read only offsets 0x00-0x65
   continue to validate unchanged, because the bytes they have not read
   were previously zero and remain ignorable.

   Offset  Len  Field         Description
   0x66     1   SPEC_REV      0 = pre-extension (block all zero);
                              1 = this revision
   0x67     1   FLAGS         bit 0 = URI_ANCHORED; all other bits
                              MUST be zero
   0x68     1   ACTION_LEN    Significant ACTION bytes; 0 = action
                              omitted
   0x69    16   ACTION        The action token (Section 4.1),
                              lowercase US-ASCII, right-padded with
                              0x00
   0x79     7   RESERVED      MUST be all zero

   *URI_ANCHORED.* Set when the frame's ROUTE_SHARD was derived from a
   URI authority (Section 4.4) rather than from any local artefact.
   Implementations that route between nodes MUST require URI_ANCHORED to
   be set; when it is clear, the ROUTE_SHARD carries no globally
   routable semantics and MAY be used only for dispatch local to a
   single sender.

   *The ACTION field.* The action of an rttp URI is an open set
   (Section 4.1); this document deliberately defines no enumeration of
   verbs, because enumerating an open set would close it.  Permitted
   characters are written to the field verbatim as US-ASCII; the
   significant length is written to ACTION_LEN; remaining bytes MUST be
   0x00.  A frame with ACTION_LEN greater than 16 MUST be rejected.



Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                  [Page 17]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


   ACTION_LEN = 0 means the action is omitted and the default operation
   of Section 4.3 applies.  ACTION and URI_ANCHORED are independent: a
   frame may carry either, both, or neither.

   *Unknown verbs.* Because the action space is open, a receiver will
   encounter verbs it does not recognise.  On encountering an
   unrecognised action verb, an implementation MUST NOT infer safety
   from the default-operation statement of Section 4.3: the verb MUST be
   treated as having unknown safety and either require explicit
   authorisation under the local security policy or be rejected
   (Section 9).

   *Rejection rules (fail closed).* A receiver MUST reject a frame if
   any of the following holds: the ACTION field contains characters
   outside the set of Section 4.1, exceeds 16 significant bytes, or
   carries non-zero padding; SPEC_REV is outside the known set; SPEC_REV
   is 0 and the extension block is not all zero; or SPEC_REV is 1 and
   RESERVED is not all zero or unknown FLAGS bits are set.

7.1.2.  Time Fields of the Pulse

   Three fields of the pulse header carry time and order.  Their
   semantics are deliberately narrow: a pulse is a claim of intent, and
   the only freshness that can authorize anything rides the answer side
   (Section 6); the pulse's time fields make the claim's moment
   checkable, not the subject's validity.

   *TIMESTAMP.* The 16-octet field at offset 0x24 is an unsigned big-
   endian count of nanoseconds since the Unix epoch
   (1970-01-01T00:00:00Z), the instant at which the pulse was emitted.
   A receiver that subtracts TIMESTAMP from its own clock obtains the
   pulse's age offline, from the bytes alone: a pulse states how old it
   is, whatever channel carried it.  A receiver MUST NOT treat
   TIMESTAMP, or the age it yields, as a statement about the subject's
   standing; the moment a pulse claims becomes decision-relevant only
   when it is checked against the lease of an answer.  Deployments MAY
   refuse pulses older than a locally configured bound; the bound is a
   deployment choice, as the lease window of Section 6.1 is.

   *TTL_PULSE.* The one-octet hop count bounds a pulse's forwarding
   life.  A sender MUST set TTL_PULSE to at least 1 when the pulse is
   intended to be forwarded; a receiver MUST NOT forward a pulse
   received with TTL_PULSE 0, and MUST decrement the field before
   forwarding.  Verification deployments that consume pulses where they
   receive them place no trust in this field.






Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                  [Page 18]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


   *SEQUENCE_ID.* The 16-octet monotonic per-sender pulse index orders a
   sender's own emissions.  A sender SHOULD assign values that never
   repeat and never decrease over the life of the AID_ORIGIN; a receiver
   MAY use the (AID_ORIGIN, SEQUENCE_ID) pair to detect duplicate or
   reordered delivery among the pulses it has observed.  The field
   carries no cross-sender meaning and no global ordering.

7.2.  The Attestation Envelope (iqa)

   The attestation envelope is the fixed 128-octet answer frame that
   carries an iqa attestation answer: the standing verdict, its lease,
   and its authentication.

   Offset  Len  Field         Description
     0      4   magic         0x49 0x51 0x41 0x45 (ASCII "IQAE")
     4      1   version       0x01 (this revision)
     5      1   algorithm     0x01 = HMAC-SHA256; 0x00 invalid;
                              other values undefined in version 1
     6      2   flags         unsigned, big-endian; unassigned;
                              sent as 0x0000
     8      8   lease_expiry  unsigned, big-endian; Unix seconds;
                              the instant until which the answer
                              counts as fresh (Section 6.1)
    16     16   intent_shard  ROUTE_SHARD of the subject
                              (Section 4.4)
    32     32   attestation   HMAC-SHA256 over the frame (below)
    64      8   organ         exactly 8 octets of US-ASCII
    72      8   nonce         unsigned, big-endian; unique per
                              verdict issued
    80      1   standing      the verdict state (below)
    81     15   reserved      MUST be all zeros
    96     32   extension     MUST be all zeros in version 1

   *The standing byte.* The octet at offset 80 takes one of four values,
   a closed set fixed in this document: 0x00 (ghost), 0x01 (probation),
   0x02 (radiant), 0x03 (genesis).  No other value is valid.  A receiver
   MUST reject a frame whose standing byte is outside this set.  The set
   is closed in version 1; extending it requires a revision of this
   document.  The semantics of the states — what each means, and whether
   and how a subject moves between them — are the business of the
   reference specification, not of this document; this document fixes
   only the wire encoding.

   *Canonical rule.* The attestation field covers the entire frame with
   the attestation field itself zeroed, keyed as specified by HMAC
   [RFC2104]:





Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                  [Page 19]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


   attestation = HMAC-SHA256(key,
       frame[0:32] || 0x00*32 || frame[64:128])

   Covering the full frame authenticates the organ tag, the nonce, and
   the standing byte as well: a rewrite of the named answerer, the
   verdict state, or a replayed frame with a swapped standing does not
   survive verification.

   *Verification procedure.* A receiver: (1) rejects the frame if its
   length is not 128, its magic is not "IQAE", its version is not 1, its
   algorithm is not 0x01, its standing byte is outside the closed set,
   its reserved or extension fields are not all zero; (2) rejects the
   frame if lease_expiry is earlier than the current time, checked
   against the receiver's own clock (Section 6.1); (3) copies the frame,
   zeroes bytes 32..63, computes HMAC-SHA256 with the organ's key
   material — carried by the verifier per [IQA-SPEC], with no directory
   and no network call — and compares in constant time; (4) interprets
   the standing byte.

   *Security properties.* Replay is mitigated by lease_expiry and by
   nonce uniqueness per organ; receivers SHOULD reject a repeated
   (organ, nonce) pair within one lease window.  The algorithm byte
   exists so that the keyed hash can be replaced without a frame
   redesign; 0x01 is the only defined value of version 1.  Section 12
   compares this construction with portable attestation formats built on
   general parser stacks: the envelope trades expressiveness for fixed-
   offset determinism, so that a verifier with nothing but SHA-256
   [FIPS180] and a key can verify with zero dependencies.

7.2.1.  Test Vector AE128-VECTOR-1

   Any implementation MUST reproduce the following frame byte for byte
   from the parameters alone, and MUST accept the frame after a round
   trip.

















Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                  [Page 20]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


   authority      = f3b2a1c4.pillar.example   (the example of
                                               Section 4.1)
   ROUTE_SHARD    = SHA-256(ASCII(authority))[0:16]
                  = 557c8154d3780cb78cc5fa1bd72b331c
   organ key      = 32-byte US-ASCII test key:
                    "PLSF-TEST-ORG-KEY-00012345678901"
                    (a label, not a name dependency)
   version        = 0x01        algorithm = 0x01
   standing       = 0x02 (radiant)          flags = 0x0000
   lease_expiry   = 1798761600              (2027-01-01T00:00:00Z)
   organ          = "ORG-TEST"              nonce = 1
   reserved/extension/attestation fields = zero before signing
   magic          = "IQAE"

   Resulting frame (128 octets):

     0  49 51 41 45 01 01 00 00 00 00 00 00 6b 36 ec 80
    16  55 7c 81 54 d3 78 0c b7 8c c5 fa 1b d7 2b 33 1c
    32  4b d1 4b 6a e7 b0 09 04 98 62 94 a3 26 a0 f0 25
    48  58 47 18 4f f2 c9 18 55 39 d4 86 3e fb 84 59 6a
    64  4f 52 47 2d 54 45 53 54 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 01
    80  02 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
    96  00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
   112  00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00

   attestation (bytes 32..63) =
     4bd14b6ae7b00904986294a326a0f0255847184ff2c9185539d4863efb84596a

8.  Attestation Response Semantics

   An attestation response — the outcome of the verification of
   Section 7.2 as consumed by clients of Section 5.5 — carries two
   fields: a refusal reason and a grant reference.  This section defines
   both; the vocabulary has been exercised by deployed implementations
   and public conformance runs (Section 12).

8.1.  Refusal Reasons

   The refusal reason is null when there is no refusal: the response is
   a permit, and the answer may be relied on under the rules of
   Section 6.  A null refusal reason is the only representation of
   "permitted"; there is no affirmative "granted" value.

   For a refusal, the reason is exactly one value from the following
   closed set, and it is the first value in the list whose condition
   applies (the priority order is part of this definition):





Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                  [Page 21]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


   *evidence_binding_mismatch* — The presented evidence is bound to a
   different grant or subject than the one in the request.

   *evidence_expired* — The lease of the presented evidence has expired
   (Section 6.1).

   *authority_not_determined* — The authority for the subject could not
   be determined at answer time — because the organ or the authority
   source could not be reached, or because the only observation
   available predates the request and therefore establishes nothing
   about the present.  An unreachable source is refused under this
   value, never read as assent.

   *authority_revoked* — The authority for the subject has been revoked.

   *operation_not_permitted* — The requested operation is not permitted
   for this subject or grant, for reasons other than the four above.

   The set is closed: implementations MUST NOT emit values outside it,
   and MUST NOT reinterpret an emitted value to mean something else.  A
   response that reports an outcome without its reason is not
   conformant: the reason is what makes a refusal auditable.

   The closed set also answers an argument from deployment practice: if
   a refusal is fatal and unexplained, sharing credentials becomes the
   rational shortcut for the blocked party.  A legible refusal — a
   closed set of reasons with an auditable receipt — gives the caller
   something to read, degrade on, retry, or reroute, and attenuation
   survives precisely because a refusal can be read, re-derived by a
   third party, and answered to.

   For the same reason, a refusal reason MUST be computed over the
   authority facts the response carries — facts a third party can re-
   derive from pinned inputs.  A refusal computed over labels, opinions,
   or unrecorded context alone is not auditable, and producing one is
   not a conformance target of this section.

8.2.  Grant Reference

   Every response — permit or refusal — names the authorisation it
   relied on.  The grant reference is a structure with the following
   members:









Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                  [Page 22]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


   grant                identifier of the grant as issued
   evidence_id          identifier of the evidence bound to it
   issued_at_ms         grant issue instant, Unix milliseconds
   expires_at_ms        grant expiry instant, Unix milliseconds
   observation_as_of_ms the as-of instant of the standing
                        observation the answer relied on, or
                        null

   The observation member deserves its own rule, because it is where an
   implementation can quietly inflate an answer: *observation_as_of_ms
   is null whenever the observation the answer relied on is absent or
   not fresh*, even if a later, successful observation is available at
   answer time.  A diagnostic or opportunistic read performed after the
   relied-on evidence expired does not backfill the member: diagnostic
   reads do not participate in authorisation and do not renew evidence.
   The member states the age of what the answer actually relied on, not
   the freshness of the freshest thing the implementation happened to
   see.

   The grant reference is also where the race boundary lives.  A
   revocation arriving just before or just after an invocation ends is a
   boundary no protocol erases; what the response owes the relying party
   is a legible record of it: the members above state when the
   authority-side facts were effective (issued_at_ms, expires_at_ms) and
   when they were observed (observation_as_of_ms).  Together with the
   evaluation rules of Section 6.3, this lets the caller decide with the
   age of its inputs on the table — an expired read is answered as
   expired, never replayed as fresh.

8.3.  Provenance of the Vocabulary

   The closed set and the priority order of Section 8.1 are defined by
   this document.  The vocabulary has been exercised in public
   conformance runs recorded by the Agent-Authority-Conformance
   laboratory of the Linux Foundation Decentralized Trust, including
   runs by implementers other than the author (Section 12); the
   laboratory records runs and certifies nothing.

8.4.  Interpreters Consume the Answer

   The refusal reason and the standing bytes of this section are what
   clocks and revocation lists compute: a lease has expired or it has
   not, the authority was revoked or it was not.  A reader that
   interprets policy — a rule engine, a human, or a probabilistic
   program — MAY consume the answer as an input and rank what is
   permitted within it; it MUST NOT overrule it.  Policy interpretation
   sorts choices among operations the authority layer has already
   allowed; it does not get a vote on whether the claimant stands.



Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                  [Page 23]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


   Two properties follow.  First, the audit target is the wire record:
   the answer is bytes a third party can re-derive from pinned inputs,
   while a model's reading of a mandate is an opinion about what the
   mandate meant — no reader can argue a timestamp into the future.
   Second, the split is what makes the schemes usable where no
   interpreter exists at all: air-gapped, degraded, and store-and-
   forward deployments have no model to ask, and fail-closed behaviour
   there requires the closed wire semantics this section defines.  If
   interpretation by language models works, it works one layer up —
   exactly where this document already places policy.

9.  Security Considerations

   The security properties of the two schemes share one foundation, and
   the following statements apply to both of them.

   *  *No lookup.* Neither scheme resolves through DNS, and neither
      performs a lookup when a URI is used: there is no resolver to
      poison, no registration to hijack, and no query metadata to
      observe on a resolution path.

   *  *No secrets in the URI.* Neither scheme defines userinfo, so
      credentials cannot be carried in one.  Operators and deployments
      MUST NOT place secrets in any component: a URI is expected to be
      logged, quoted, and rendered.

   *  *Unknown actions carry unknown safety.* The safe default
      operations of Sections 4.3 and 5.3 apply to the omitted-action
      forms only.  An implementation MUST NOT infer safety for an
      unrecognised action verb; it MUST treat the verb as having unknown
      safety and either require explicit authorisation under the local
      security policy or reject it.

   *  *No confidentiality, authentication, or transport security.*
      Neither scheme protects a URI in transit, and neither turns a URI
      into a proof: signing is not encryption, and a URI is not a
      signature.

   *  *Parsing establishes nothing.* Neither the syntax nor any
      component of a URI of either scheme is evidence about its subject,
      and a client MUST NOT present a parsed or rendered URI as if it
      were evidence (Sections 4.5 and 5.5).









Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                  [Page 24]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


   *  *Fail closed, everywhere.* Both wire formats of Section 7 reject
      unknown versions, unknown fields, and wrong lengths rather than
      skipping them; the response semantics of Section 8 report an
      unreachable source as a refusal rather than as assent; and the
      lease of Section 6 expires by default.  At no decision point does
      silence, absence, or an unrecognised input resolve to "yes".

   The scheme-specific considerations follow.

9.1.  The rttp scheme

   *  An rttp URI is a *claim of intent directed at a subject*.  The
      derived address is an *entry fingerprint, not a proof of
      identity*.  Identity is carried by the subject's AID, and any
      attestation of it is carried separately.

   *  *The 128-bit truncation, stated honestly.* The derived address is
      the first 16 octets of a SHA-256 digest (Section 4.4).  What the
      construction defends against is substitution of the authority in
      use — finding a second authority that yields the same address —
      which costs approximately 2^128 operations.  It does not defend
      against collision search in the abstract: a birthday collision
      exists at approximately 2^64, and reaching it additionally
      requires a second, independent party to adopt the colliding label
      — two gates, not one.  These bounds are the design's honest
      account, not a guarantee of collision-freedom.

   *  *Display forms are not identifiers.* The 8-hex-digit display forms
      of both schemes (the rttp hash-intent and the short iqa subject
      form) fix a 32-bit space, whose birthday bound — collisions
      expected after roughly 2^16 adoptions — makes them unfit as sole
      identifiers.  They are display conveniences over the full hash
      forms and MUST NOT be used as the sole identifier of a subject
      (Sections 4.1 and 5.1).

   *  The authority is *pseudonymous, not anonymous*.  It is a stable
      name and will appear in logs, in caches, and in anything that
      quotes the URI.  Whether that name is linkable to a subject is a
      property of the operator's naming choices, not of the scheme.

9.2.  The iqa scheme

   *  An iqa URI is a *claim about the attestation standing of a named
      subject*.  Neither the syntax nor any component of the URI is
      evidence of standing.






Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                  [Page 25]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


   *  *Seal forgery.* Standing is carried by a keyed message
      authentication code over the subject's identity material and its
      deployment parameters (Section 7.2), not by the URI; no key
      material is ever present in an iqa URI.

   *  *Subject spoofing.* A seal presented for one subject fails binding
      when replayed for another, because the binding covers hardware and
      deployment parameters of the subject; a client MUST NOT treat a
      syntactically valid subject as a verified one.

   *  *Silence is not assent.* An endpoint that is unreachable, times
      out, or returns an error MUST NOT be read as affirmative standing:
      absence of evidence is not evidence of compliance.  The refusal
      vocabulary of Section 8.1 gives this rule a wire representation:
      the value authority_not_determined.

   *  *Lease and replay.* The lease of Section 6 bounds how long an
      answer may be relied on; the nonce of Section 7.2 makes each
      verdict unique per organ.  A repeated (organ, nonce) pair within
      one lease window SHOULD be rejected.

   *  *Linkability and disclosure of interest.* An iqa URI names the
      subject being attested, so citing one discloses which identity is
      of interest, and querying several organs for the same subject is
      trivially correlatable.  *This scheme cannot be used for anonymous
      reference.* Deployments SHOULD prefer the routing-hash form over
      readable labels, SHOULD NOT encode personal identifiers in the
      action, and SHOULD treat iqa URIs in logs as an identity
      assertion.

   *  *Downgrade and scheme confusion.* No "iqas" variant exists and no
      fallback is defined.  A client that does not implement this scheme
      MUST fail closed and MUST NOT silently rewrite an iqa URI as some
      other scheme.

   *  *Detection of observers.* A measurement requested by the audit
      action compares observed execution timing against an expected
      path: execution slower than predicted is treated as evidence of an
      attached observer, and measurable deviation is itself the
      detector.  This is a property of the answering organ, not of the
      URI syntax.

   *  *Replay across epochs.* Standing material is rotated on a defined
      cycle, so a previously valid answer can become invalid without any
      change to the URI; a client MUST NOT treat a cached answer as
      current indefinitely.





Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                  [Page 26]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


   *  *Cryptographic suite.* The current construction uses a keyed
      symmetric hash rather than a public-key signature, and is
      therefore not directly affected by quantum algorithms that break
      factoring or discrete logarithms.

10.  Privacy Considerations

   The privacy properties of the two schemes share one foundation: no
   component is defined for a query string, so neither scheme offers a
   channel for a page to smuggle unrelated data into a request, and
   using a URI of either scheme does not by itself cause network traffic
   to a third party; the authority is a stable pseudonym, expected to be
   logged, quoted and rendered, and readable labels are a naming choice
   rather than a scheme property.

   Derivation, not assignment, has a privacy consequence of its own:
   because addresses are computed from labels an operator already
   controls and no registry assigns or lists them, the set of
   participants is not enumerable from the scheme, and there is no
   registration record to subpoena, scrape, or leak.  And because using
   a URI involves no query, use leaves no resolution-time trail: nothing
   observes that a particular authority was derived or cited.

   What remains correlatable is stated plainly.  The authority itself is
   a stable pseudonym whose linkability is the operator's choice
   (Section 9.1).  For "iqa", citing a URI discloses which subject is of
   interest, and the disclosure considerations of Section 9.2 apply.
   The lease of Section 6 bounds how long a cached attestation answer
   remains reliable inside a verifier; it does not bound how long a log
   retains the URI that produced the request, which is the deployer's
   retention policy.

   A client that renders such a URI SHOULD avoid prefetching, handing
   the string to third-party services, or otherwise distributing it
   beyond what the user's action requires.

11.  IANA Considerations

   IANA is requested to register the two URI schemes below, "rttp" and
   "iqa", in the "Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) Schemes" registry,
   following the template of Section 7.4 of [RFC7595] and the guidance
   of [RFC8126].  The templates below are complete.  If this document is
   approved for publication as an RFC, IANA is requested to point both
   registry entries at that RFC.







Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                  [Page 27]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


   This document creates no new IANA registries.  The wire formats of
   Section 7 are self-describing — each begins with a fixed magic value
   and an explicit version field — and the refusal vocabulary of
   Section 8 is a closed set defined entirely within this document.

11.1.  The "rttp" URI Scheme

   Scheme name: rttp

   Status: Provisional

   Applications/protocols that use this scheme name: URIs of this scheme
   name a claim of intent directed at an identified subject.
   Applications include intent-addressed requests between autonomous
   software agents and the client-side handling of such URIs by protocol
   handlers in browsers and operating systems.  The scheme defines
   addressing only; it does not define a transport or a discovery
   mechanism.

   Contact: ShaoBao Li <mailto:lee@rttp.com>

   Change controller: RTTP.COM Organization

   References: This document, and AICENT-002, the reference
   specification of the scheme [RTTP-SPEC].

   Registered with CRI scheme number 27.

11.2.  The "iqa" URI Scheme

   Scheme name: iqa

   Status: Provisional

   Applications/protocols that use this scheme name: URIs of this scheme
   name are subject-attestation references: an iqa URI names the
   attestation standing of a subject as reported by one of three named
   authority organs, without carrying the underlying cryptographic
   proof.  It is used by the reference implementations and by tools that
   cite an attestation in a document, a configuration file or a log.
   The scheme defines addressing and client behaviour only; it does not
   define a transport, a discovery mechanism, or the attestation
   algorithm.

   Contact: ShaoBao Li <mailto:lee@iqa.org>

   Change controller: IQA.ORG Organization




Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                  [Page 28]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


   References: This document, and AICENT-009, the reference
   specification of the scheme [IQA-SPEC].

   Registered with CRI scheme number 28.

12.  Related Work

   This section positions the two schemes against the specifications
   they are most often compared with.  None of the relationships below
   is a normative dependency.

   *Intent-Based Networking* [RFC9315] establishes intent as a first-
   class concept: a declarative statement of what a system should
   achieve, verified by assurance loops rather than assumed.  The
   schemes of this document take the next step on the same path: they
   make an intent addressable and attestable rather than merely stated.
   The relationship is complementary: IBN defines what an intent is; the
   schemes define where an intent claim is addressed and whether the
   claimant stands verified, and they carry no network configuration
   semantics.

   *Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs)* [W3C-DID] anchor a subject's
   identity in a resolvable, method-specific identifier, paired with
   Verifiable Credentials for portable claims.  The schemes of this
   document answer different questions: an rttp address is not assigned
   and not resolvable — it is derived from the authority string and
   consulted through no method, no registry, and no network call — and
   an iqa answer is bound to a named organ rather than to a credential
   issuer.  The two compose rather than compete: a deployment MAY anchor
   operator identity in DIDs while rttp addresses intents and iqa
   answers standing.

   *Transport and authorization infrastructure.* The schemes define
   addressing and verification semantics, not transport: the frames of
   Section 7 may be carried by HTTP [RFC9110], TLS [RFC9846], QUIC
   [RFC9000], gRPC, or any channel that preserves frame integrity; no
   transport is required and none is excluded.  Deployment authorization
   machinery — identity providers, OAuth 2.0 scopes and grants
   [RFC6749], mTLS client authentication, or capability tokens — belongs
   to the calling layer (Section 6.2); the frames carry intent claims
   and verification answers, and no bearer credential.










Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                  [Page 29]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


   *CBOR Web Token (CWT)* [RFC8392] and *Remote Attestation procedures
   (RATS)* [RFC9334] solve portable attestation and evidence with
   general parser stacks and rich claim vocabularies.  The attestation
   envelope of Section 7.2 trades expressiveness for fixed-offset
   determinism: a verifier with nothing but SHA-256 and a key can verify
   with zero dependencies.  Where rich claims are needed, those formats
   remain the right tools.

   *The W3C AI Agent Protocol Community Group* [W3C-AP-CG] has discussed
   the distinction this document's claims follow: evidence freshness,
   authority validity, and action-time authorization as three separately
   scoreable axes.  This document claims the first two (Sections 6 and
   8) and deliberately does not claim the third: authorization decisions
   belong to the calling layer, and the schemes' job is to make the
   verification answers trustworthy and cheap.  For the same reason this
   document defines no open enumeration of action verbs — the actions of
   "iqa" are a closed set of organ operations (Section 5.4), and the
   action of "rttp" is an open token that this document deliberately
   leaves unpopulated — it defines no vocabulary for policy text:
   standardizing the constraints someone happened to think of first
   would close an open set.  Policy vocabularies are deployments' own
   and belong to the calling layer.  Appendix A complements this section
   with a per-exchange cost comparison against alternative stacks.

   *Agent Authorization Envelope (AAE)* [AAE] specifies a machine-
   evaluable authorization container for autonomous agents: what the
   agent is mandated to do, under what constraints, and for how long.
   AAE answers what an agent may do; the schemes of this document answer
   where intent is addressed and whether the claimant is verified.  The
   two compose naturally — an authorization envelope can name actions on
   subjects addressed by rttp URIs and cite iqa attestations as evidence
   — and neither depends on the other.

   *Delegation policy.* Known delegation systems express constraints in
   the delegation certificate itself — caveats in one family, policy in
   another — and report a refusal to the invoker.  No deployed system
   this document is aware of reports to the delegator, and none carries
   a standard place for the reason a specific policy was violated or
   excepted.  This document does not fill that slot either, and the
   omission is deliberate: the delegator's standing instructions and
   their exceptions are calling-layer artifacts, not authority facts.
   What the schemes contribute is the receipt side: when an exception is
   exercised, the grant reference (Section 8.2) records what the answer
   relied on and when, so the exception is auditable after the fact by
   whoever is entitled to read it — the delegator learns from the
   receipt when the delegator chooses to look, not because the verifier
   pushes.  Naming the delegator-reporting slot as an open problem is,
   as of this revision, where the problem stands.



Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                  [Page 30]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


   *Agent Passport System (APS)* [APS] specifies verifiable authority,
   lifecycle, enforcement and evidence for AI agents, separating agent
   identity, represented principal, delegated authority, policy approval
   and observed results.  The attestation response vocabulary of
   Section 8 is stated in the form in which it was exercised by the
   lease-revocation-axes corpus of the Agent-Authority-Conformance
   laboratory of the Linux Foundation Decentralized Trust, whose initial
   corpus builds on this family of specifications; independent runs
   against that corpus, including the author's own, are public.  Run
   records for the corpus, including independent re-executions, are
   publicly archived.  The laboratory records runs and does not certify
   implementations; the citation reflects that posture.

13.  Internationalization Considerations

   The canonical form of a URI in either scheme is lowercase US-ASCII,
   and no international form is defined: a client MUST NOT map a Unicode
   label to its ASCII form (for example, by case folding or by applying
   an IDNA-style transformation) in order to accept it, and MUST NOT
   render such a URI as an IRI.  This is deliberate: with no host to
   resolve there is no need for a label-to-ASCII transformation, and
   permitting one would introduce a second way to write one address.

   engagement.  He pressed this revision's claims directly and
   successively, and his questions and corrections shaped it: the
   credential-sharing argument that the rationale of Section 8.1 now
   records; the observation that no deployed system carries the
   delegator's standing policy — the gap that Section 12 names and
   deliberately leaves open; and the correction that separated the
   moment a policy is expressed from the moment its condition is judged,
   which this revision adopts as the evaluation rule of Section 6.3.
   The revision is stronger for the pressure.

   decided one is the separation Section 8.1 fixes as a value of its
   own; his requirement that a recorded decision name the grant as it
   stood when it was made is the rule Section 8.2 codifies; and his
   refinement that one window opens per successful read is the sharper
   form of the fail-closed rules of Section 6.2.

   The author also thanks Tetsuroh Hori, whose clean-room recomputation
   over the frozen vectors of the family, filed in the laboratory's
   records without any prior contact with the author, is the strongest
   kind of external treatment the schemes can receive — and the one
   publishing the vectors byte-replayably was for.

Appendix A.  Comparison with Alternative Agent-to-Agent Stacks

   This appendix is informational.  It compares one concrete question-
   and-answer exchange — "may this subject, identified only by its
   shard, perform this intent?" — across four agent-to-agent stacks: A2A
   over HTTPS with OAuth 2.0, A2A with DID/VC identity, A2A with a
   capability token, and the rttp/iqa pair specified in this document.
   Each stack is scored across eleven fields that a trust-bearing
   exchange must address: discovery, identity, intent, authentication,
   attestation, authorization, delegation, replay, revocation, audit,
   and routing.

   The counts are per single exchange and assume a cold, honest
   deployment of each stack.  "Network round-trips" counts messages that
   leave the verifying party.  "Third parties" counts distinct online
   services whose response the exchange depends on.  "Real cryptographic
   steps" counts operations whose inputs and keys are local and whose
   result is checkable offline afterwards.

   +=============+=============+=========+========+====================+
   | Stack       | Network     | Third   | Real   | Offline-verifiable |
   |             | round-trips | parties | crypto | result             |
   |             |             |         | steps  |                    |
   +=============+=============+=========+========+====================+
   | A2A +       | 5           | 8       | 0      | no                 |
   | HTTPS/      |             |         |        |                    |
   | OAuth       |             |         |        |                    |
   +-------------+-------------+---------+--------+--------------------+
   | A2A + DID/  | 6           | 8       | 0      | no                 |
   | VC          |             |         |        |                    |
   +-------------+-------------+---------+--------+--------------------+
   | A2A +       | 2           | 3       | 0      | no                 |
   | capability  |             |         |        |                    |
   | token       |             |         |        |                    |
   +-------------+-------------+---------+--------+--------------------+
   | A2A +       | 0           | 0       | 7      | yes                |
   | rttp/iqa    |             |         |        |                    |
   | (this       |             |         |        |                    |
   | document)   |             |         |        |                    |
   +-------------+-------------+---------+--------+--------------------+

                  Table 2: Totals per stack (one exchange)




Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                  [Page 35]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


     +================+=============+========+============+==========+
     | Field          | HTTPS/OAuth | DID/VC | Capability | rttp/iqa |
     +================+=============+========+============+==========+
     | discovery      | 1 · 3       | 1 · 2  | 1 · 2      | 0 · 0    |
     +----------------+-------------+--------+------------+----------+
     | identity       | 0 · 0       | 1 · 1  | 0 · 0      | 0 · 0    |
     +----------------+-------------+--------+------------+----------+
     | intent         | 0 · 0       | 0 · 0  | 0 · 0      | 0 · 0    |
     +----------------+-------------+--------+------------+----------+
     | authentication | 1 · 2       | 1 · 1  | 0 · 0      | 0 · 0    |
     +----------------+-------------+--------+------------+----------+
     | attestation    | 0 · 0       | 0 · 1  | 0 · 0      | 0 · 0    |
     +----------------+-------------+--------+------------+----------+
     | authorization  | 0 · 0       | 0 · 0  | 0 · 0      | 0 · 0    |
     +----------------+-------------+--------+------------+----------+
     | delegation     | 1 · 1       | 0 · 0  | 0 · 0      | 0 · 0    |
     +----------------+-------------+--------+------------+----------+
     | replay         | 0 · 0       | 1 · 1  | 0 · 0      | 0 · 0    |
     +----------------+-------------+--------+------------+----------+
     | revocation     | 1 · 1       | 1 · 1  | 0 · 0      | 0 · 0    |
     +----------------+-------------+--------+------------+----------+
     | audit          | 0 · 0       | 0 · 0  | 0 · 0      | 0 · 0    |
     +----------------+-------------+--------+------------+----------+
     | routing        | 1 · 1       | 1 · 1  | 1 · 1      | 0 · 0    |
     +----------------+-------------+--------+------------+----------+
     | totals         | 5 · 8       | 6 · 8  | 2 · 3      | 0 · 0    |
     +----------------+-------------+--------+------------+----------+

       Table 3: Per-field cost (network round-trips · third parties)

   Three caveats keep the comparison honest.  First, the capability-
   token stack is also offline at verification time; its weakness is
   different — a capability confers authority but states nothing about
   the bearer's standing, and its only revocation is expiry.  Second,
   DID/VC provides strong identity and portable audit artifacts; its
   freshness and revocation paths re-introduce network calls to the
   issuer or a status list.  Third, rttp/iqa intentionally omits
   discovery and delegation in this revision: routing is derived rather
   than resolved, and delivery of a frame to its shard remains an
   operator concern.  The counts describe the verification of one
   answer, not the provisioning of the system that produced it.

   The structural claim the tables support is narrow: in the rttp/iqa
   stack the material needed to decide — and, after the fact, to re-
   verify — a standing verdict is contained entirely in the two frames,
   so no online party is required at either moment.  Whether that
   property is worth the corresponding loss of discovery infrastructure
   is a deployment decision, not a claim of this document.



Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                  [Page 36]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


A.1.  Delegation and Attenuation

   The single-exchange comparison above deliberately excludes
   delegation.  This section records a second, harder experiment: Agent
   A grants Agent B authority to approve invoices up to EUR 10,000;
   Agent B attenuates that grant to EUR 2,000 and further delegates
   execution to a Payment Agent.  Each stack is observed on nine
   delegation-specific fields: the grant, the attenuation, the further
   delegation, chain verification, subject binding, standing, replay,
   revocation, and the audit artifact.  The scorecard below records all
   nine fields, together with one cross-cutting observation — where each
   stack's delegation root lives.  A live demonstration of this
   delegation experiment, covering all nine fields, is public at the
   reference specification's site [DEMOS], among the further live
   demonstrations hosted there.  The observations are informational and
   indicate typical deployments, not normative requirements of any
   stack.

   +============+=============+============+===========+===============+
   |Field       |HTTPS/OAuth  |DID/VC      |Capability | rttp/iqa      |
   +============+=============+============+===========+===============+
   |the grant   |a coarse     |A issues a  |a root     | an intent     |

        Table 4: Delegation scorecard (EUR 10,000 granted, EUR 2,000
                             delegated onward)

   Three observations.  First, the capability stack is the only one in
   which attenuation is a native operation; its corresponding weakness
   is that the credential carries authority without context — no
   standing, no identity assertion, and revocation only by expiry.
   Second, in the rttp and iqa stack the delegation gap is explicit and
   stated: the AE-128 layout (Section 7.2) allocates no amount field,
   and delegation is not specified in this revision, so attenuation
   cannot enter the frame and must be performed at the application
   layer.  Two compositions have been demonstrated in that role: re-
   attestation, in which the organ issues a fresh envelope for the
   delegatee's own subject; and a capability wrapper whose root caveat



Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                  [Page 38]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


   embeds the (subject, intent, organ, standing, time, proof) audit
   tuple, so that the standing context travels with the attenuated
   grant.  Both are application-layer work; neither is specified here.
   Third, the re-attestation chain has an honest shape limitation worth
   stating plainly: two envelopes anchored at the same organ are two
   independent attestations, not a linked proof that B's attenuation
   authorized the Payment Agent's envelope.

   The practical conclusion is narrow and symmetrical: for attenuation,
   the capability construction is the natural tool; for carrying
   verifiable standing with the grant, the envelopes specified in this
   document are.  The two are composable, and the composition does not
   require changes to either frame format.

Appendix B.  Changes from draft-li-rttp-iqa-addressing-01

   This appendix is informational and is intended to be removed if this
   document is published as an RFC.

   *  Added Section 6.3, Evaluation at the Moment of Use: the
      delegation-time and invocation-time moments are separated, and the
      boundary race around revocation is stated with its receipt-side
      treatment.

   *  Added to Section 6.2 the mid-task statement: conditions that must
      hold at every use are re-checked at each use, armed by the lease
      expiry the verifier already holds.

   *  Added to Section 8.1 the rationale for legible refusal —
      credential sharing as the failure mode of fatal silence — and the
      rule that refusal reasons are computed over re-derivable authority
      facts.

   *  Added to Section 8.2 the statement that the grant reference
      records when the authority-side facts were effective and when they
      were observed.

   *  Added Section 8.4, Interpreters Consume the Answer: policy
      interpreters rank within the answer and do not overrule it; the
      audit target is the wire record; the closed wire semantics cover
      deployments without interpreters.

   *  Added to Section 12 the policy-vocabulary open-set note, the
      delegator-reporting open problem, and a note that corpus run
      records, including independent re-executions, are publicly
      archived.





Li                         Expires 5 May 2027                  [Page 39]

Internet-Draft          rttp and iqa URI Schemes           November 2026


   *  Added to Section 12 the Intent-Based Networking paragraph
      [RFC9315], positioning the schemes as making intents addressable
      and attestable rather than merely stated.

   *  Extended the references: added the rttp scheme reference
      specification [RTTP-SPEC] and [RFC9315], retargeted [IQA-SPEC] at
      its canonical site, and retitled [DEMOS] to cover both schemes.

   *  Added to the Acknowledgements the public discussion that produced
      the above.

   *  Added Section 4.5.4, No Lookup: the requirement asserted in
      Section 4.4 now has its client-requirements home, and
      Section 5.5's summary lists it.  A sentence in the introduction of
      Section 4.5, carried over from earlier revisions with its
      beginning lost, is repaired.

   *  Corrected the standing-state sentence of Section 7.2: whether a
      subject moves between states is itself deferred to the reference
      specification, not asserted; the wire encoding is unchanged.
